findings.title: Reclaim cron never commits — reclaimer is a silent no-op
findings.why_it_matters: The cron entrypoint opens a session with `_ctx_session(ctx)`, calls the two reclaimers, and returns. Both reclaimers only `flush()` (report_tasks.py:249, 307); nothing in this call chain ever calls `db.commit()`, and the session is never closed either. When the session object is garbage-collected, SQLAlchemy rolls the open transaction back, so every FAILED marking and every RECLAIMED audit row is discarded. Observable behavior: after an ARQ worker is OOM-killed mid-render, the report_files row stays PENDING and the frontend polls forever — exactly the scenario this cron was added to fix (its own docstring says so). Nothing errors, so no log line ever reveals it. The tests cannot catch it: tests/workers/test_report_tasks.py:306-345 and 511-557 call `reclaim_stale_tasks(db, ...)` / `reclaim_stale_execution_logs(db, ...)` directly with the test's own session, never through `reclaim_stale_report_tasks(ctx)` — a classic stand-in guard gap where the test's context is more forgiving than the thing it guards. The fix is to reuse `worker.session_scope` (the wrapper both task bodies already use for exactly this 'remembering to close is memory, not structure' reason) and commit after both reclaimers.
evidence: pcs-backend/app/workers/report_tasks.py:323-328 — `db: AsyncSession = _ctx_session(ctx)` / `await reclaim_stale_tasks(db, older_than_minutes=STALE_MINUTES)` / `await reclaim_stale_execution_logs(db, older_than_minutes=STALE_MINUTES)` — no `commit()`, no `close()` anywhere in the function.

pcs-backend/app/workers/report_tasks.py:249 — `    await db.flush()` (end of reclaim_stale_tasks); pcs-backend/app/workers/report_tasks.py:307 — `    await db.flush()` (end of reclaim_stale_execution_logs). Both rely on a caller that never commits.
pcs-backend/app/db/session.py:71-85 — `get_async_session_factory` builds a plain `async_sessionmaker` with no autocommit; there is no ambient commit hook that could rescue the flush.

tests/workers/test_report_tasks.py:306 — `n = await reclaim_stale_tasks(db, older_than_minutes=15)` — the tests pass the fixture session directly and never exercise the cron wrapper, so the missing commit is invisible to CI.

Contrast with the task bodies, which do commit explicitly and are tested for it: report_tasks.py:172 `            await db.commit()`, and tests/workers/test_report_tasks.py:381 `test_failure_state_is_committed_not_just_left_in_the_session`.
findings.suggested_fix:
In `reclaim_stale_report_tasks`, use the existing `worker.session_scope` context manager and commit once after both reclaimers:

```python
async def reclaim_stale_report_tasks(ctx) -> None:
    from app.workers.worker import session_scope  # local import: circular (worker imports this module)
    async with session_scope(ctx) as db:
        await reclaim_stale_tasks(db, older_than_minutes=STALE_MINUTES)
        await reclaim_stale_execution_logs(db, older_than_minutes=STALE_MINUTES)
        await db.commit()
```
Also add a test that calls `reclaim_stale_report_tasks(ctx)` with an injected `session_factory` and then reads `ReportFile.status` from a *separate* session — mirroring the two existing `_is_committed` tests — so the commit is covered by the same observation point the task bodies already use.

findings.title: Successful executions never reach FINISHED; reclaimer corrupts their audit row
findings.why_it_matters: The task sets `task_row.status = "RUNNING"` at line 83, but no code path in `execute_definition_task` ever writes `"FINISHED"` — neither on the success path (lines 86-96) nor after the REPORT_EXECUTED audit (lines 133-142). So every completed execution is left in the DB with status RUNNING forever. The status endpoint papers over this by synthesizing FINISHED from `report_file_id` (report_builder.py:296), so the happy path looks fine and the bug hides. The damage lands on the reclaimer: `reclaim_stale_execution_logs` selects `status IN ('QUEUED','RUNNING')` with an `or_(updated_at < cutoff, created_at < cutoff)` arm, so 15 minutes after a *successful* run its row matches. It then sets status='FAILED', overwrites `condition_snapshot` with reclaim_reason — destroying the reproducible record of what was actually queried — and writes a REPORT_FAILED audit entry for a run that produced a file. That is precisely the audit tampering the function's own docstring says it avoids ('FINISHED / FAILED 已是终态，再动它们就是篡改审计记录'): the guard is dead code because the terminal state it protects is never written.
evidence: pcs-backend/app/workers/report_builder_tasks.py:93-96 — `            file_id = await _render_and_store(` / `                db, out=out, project_id=pid, job_id=job_id, task_id=job_id,` / `                output_format=out.snapshot.get("output_format") or "pdf")` / `            await db.commit()` — the success path commits without ever setting `task_row.status = "FINISHED"`.

pcs-backend/app/workers/report_builder_tasks.py:112 — `            if attempt_no >= MAX_TRIES and task_row is not None:` — the only place `task_row.status` is assigned after the initial RUNNING, and it only ever assigns FAILED.

pcs-backend/app/api/v1/report_builder.py:296 — `    status = "FINISHED" if row.report_file_id else (row.status or "QUEUED")` — the DB column is never read as FINISHED, which is why the missing write is invisible.

pcs-backend/app/workers/report_tasks.py:284-285 — `            ReportExecutionLog.status.in_(("QUEUED", "RUNNING")),` / `            or_(ReportExecutionLog.updated_at < cutoff,` — the reclaim predicate a completed (still RUNNING) row satisfies.
pcs-backend/app/models/report.py:211 — comment="QUEUED 已入队 / RUNNING 执行中 / FINISHED 已出文件 / FAILED 已终结（含被回收）" — FINISHED is a defined terminal state that is never produced.
findings.suggested_fix:
Set the terminal state on the success path in `execute_definition_task`, immediately before the REPORT_EXECUTED commit (line 141):

```python
        if task_row is not None:
            task_row.status = "FINISHED"
        await audit.write(action=AuditAction.REPORT_EXECUTED, ...)
        await db.commit()
```
`task_row` is still attached after the commit on line 96 (no rollback happened on that path), so no re-fetch is needed. After this, `reclaim_stale_execution_logs`'s `status IN ('QUEUED','RUNNING')` filter starts meaning what its docstring claims, and report_builder.py:296's synthesis becomes a redundant-but-harmless safety net. Add a test asserting a successful `execute_definition_task` leaves `status == 'FINISHED'` when read from a separate session, and that `reclaim_stale_execution_logs` skips it.

findings.title: Printed QR carries no signature; verify endpoint always 403s
findings.why_it_matters: The QR verification path is unwired end to end in this diff. First, no QR is ever rendered: `_render_sync` hardcodes `qr_payload=None`, so `renderer_pdf`'s `if qr_payload:` branch (renderer_pdf.py:256) never runs and no PDF contains a QR code. Second, even if it did, `build_qr_payload` emits `{base}/api/v1/report/verify/{report_id}#{json}` with no `?sig=…&exp=…`, and the only producer of that HMAC signature in the entire repository is tests/api/v1/test_report.py:49-51. `_check_sig` fail-closed, so every scan of every printed QR returns 403 '签名无效'. The tests are green because they hand-build a correct signature, which is a stand-in guard that does not mirror the production path. Field verification is a stated P8 deliverable; today a scanner at a plant gets a guaranteed 403.
evidence: pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:220 — `                          qr_payload=None, assumed_fields=[], context=ctx)` — the render call hardcodes None, so renderer_pdf.py:256 `    if qr_payload:` is never true.
grep for `build_qr_payload` across the repo returns only its definition (qr.py:25) and tests/services/report/test_report_service.py — zero production callers.
grep for `report_verify_secret` returns app/api/v1/report.py:100 (verification), app/core/config.py:79/169/176 (config), tests/api/v1/test_report.py:49 (test-side signing) — no production signer.

pcs-backend/app/api/v1/report.py:107-110 — `    expect = hmac.new(secret.encode(), f"{report_file_id}:{exp}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()` / `    if not hmac.compare_digest(expect, sig or ""):` / `        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="签名无效")` — fail-closed, correct, and unsatisfiable for any URL a QR could carry.
pcs-backend/app/services/report/qr.py:43 — `    return (f"{verify_base_url.rstrip('/')}/api/v1/report/verify/{report_id}#"` — the payload builder emits no sig/exp query parameters.
findings.suggested_fix: Two coordinated changes, both in `report_service`. (1) Add a signer next to `qr.py` that mints the short-lived signature: `def sign_verify_url(*, report_file_id, exp) -> str` computing `hmac.new(settings.report_verify_secret.encode(), f"{report_file_id}:{exp}".encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()` — reuse the exact input format from `_check_sig` (report.py:107) rather than re-deriving it. (2) In `store_rendered`/`generate`, build `exp = int(now.timestamp()) + VERIFY_TTL_S` and pass a real payload through `_render_sync(..., qr_payload=build_qr_payload(..., verify_base_url=f"{base}/api/v1/report/verify/{row_id}?sig={sig}&exp={exp}"))` — note this requires the report_file_id, which today is only known *after* `_upsert_report_file`, so the ordering in `store_rendered` (render → hash → write → upsert) needs to become (upsert PENDING row → sign with its id → render → write). Because the signature is time-varying it must NOT feed `_content_hash`, or the determinism guarantee that `qr.py`'s docstring rests on (same content ⇒ same hash ⇒ dedup works) breaks; keep the hash over (blocks, style, output_format, ctx) as it is and let the QR vary. If signed URLs are genuinely deferred, delete `qr.py` and the `verify` route together rather than shipping a 403-by-construction endpoint.

findings.title: Builder enqueues before committing its log row — orphan file race
findings.why_it_matters: The execute endpoint enqueues the ARQ job first (line 328) and only afterwards inserts the ReportExecutionLog row and commits (lines 348-368). The worker can therefore pick the job up before that commit lands: `execute_definition_task` looks up the log by `task_id` (report_builder_tasks.py:75), gets None, skips setting RUNNING, and `_link_report_file`'s UPDATE (report_builder_tasks.py:247-250) matches zero rows. The job still succeeds and the file is registered, but nothing links it to the task_id. Observable behavior: the client polls `/executions/{task_id}`, the row now exists with status QUEUED and report_file_id NULL, and it never resolves — the frontend polls to timeout while a perfectly good file sits in the DB unreachable from this task. The window is small (one insert + commit after Redis has already been handed the job) but the worker is polling Redis continuously, so a busy worker can win it. The sibling endpoint in report.py already solves exactly this by choosing `task_id` first and passing `_job_id=task_id` so the row can be committed before the job exists.
evidence: pcs-backend/app/api/v1/report_builder.py:328 — `    task_id = await arq_queue.enqueue_definition_execution(` — the job is on the queue before the log row exists.
pcs-backend/app/api/v1/report_builder.py:368 — `    await db.commit()      # 端点负责 commit（与本仓其它写端点一致）` — the log row (added at line 348) is only durable here, after the enqueue.

pcs-backend/app/workers/report_builder_tasks.py:75-76 — `        task_row = (await db.execute(_sel(_Log).where(` / `            _Log.task_id == job_id))).scalar_one_or_none()` — a miss here makes both the RUNNING update and the later backfill no-ops.

pcs-backend/app/workers/report_builder_tasks.py:229 — `    await _link_report_file(db, task_id=task_id, report_file_id=row.report_file_id)` — the UPDATE at 247-250 silently affects 0 rows; there is no rowcount check.

Parallel pattern already in this diff: pcs-backend/app/api/v1/report.py:161 `    task_id = uuid.uuid4().hex` … :189 `_job_id=task_id,` — the generate endpoint commits the PENDING row *before* enqueueing.
`enqueue_definition_execution` (arq_queue.py:81-85) does not forward a `_job_id`, so the task id cannot currently be chosen by the caller on this path.
findings.suggested_fix:
Mirror report.py's ordering. Add a `job_id` parameter to `enqueue_definition_execution` that is forwarded to `pool.enqueue_job` as `_job_id` (arq_queue.py:49), then in the endpoint:

```python
task_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
db.add(ReportExecutionLog(..., task_id=task_id, ...))
await db.commit()          # row is durable before the job exists
try:
    task_id = await arq_queue.enqueue_definition_execution(job_id=task_id, ...)
except Exception:
    ...  # mark the row FAILED rather than leaving an orphan QUEUED row
    raise
```
This also fixes the secondary issue that a 503 from `_enqueue` currently leaves a committed QUEUED log row with no task id the client ever received — the report.py endpoint already handles that with its `_fail_pending` helper; port that idea.

findings.title: Verify rate limit is per-process on an unauthenticated endpoint
findings.why_it_matters: `/verify/{id}` is the one unauthenticated route in the P8 surface (免登录), and its only brute-force/abuse protection is `check_rate_limit`, an in-process dict guarded by a module-level asyncio.Lock. With N uvicorn workers the effective limit is N × `report_verify_rate_limit`, and the states are not shared — so the protection is weakest exactly in the horizontally-scaled deployment it is most needed in. Separately, `_WINDOW_STATE.setdefault(key, deque())` never removes keys: eviction happens only inside a request for that same key, and the only other entry point is `clear_all_rate_limits()` (test/ops only). An unauthenticated attacker rotating source IPs grows the dict without bound for the process lifetime. The pre-existing implementation is documented as single-instance-only; the finding is that this new public endpoint inherits that limitation without a compensating control (no signature check happens before the limiter, so unauthenticated callers can consume the window).
evidence: pcs-backend/app/api/v1/report.py:269-271 — `    if not await check_rate_limit(f"report_verify:{ip}",` / `                                  limit=get_settings().report_verify_rate_limit,` / `                                  window_seconds=60):` — the unauthenticated route's only guard.

pcs-backend/app/services/_sliding_window_rate_limit.py:5-6 — module docstring: "适用 single-instance 部署 … 多实例需换 Redis-backed 实现 (TODO: deploy multi-instance 时替换)" — the limit is per-process by construction (`_WINDOW_STATE: Final[dict[str, deque[float]]]`).

pcs-backend/app/services/_sliding_window_rate_limit.py:37 — `        dq = _WINDOW_STATE.setdefault(key, deque())` — a key is created per client IP and is never deleted; the only removal path is `clear_all_rate_limits()`.
pcs-backend/app/api/v1/report.py:275 — `    _check_sig(report_file_id, sig, exp)` runs *after* the limiter, so an unauthenticated caller with no valid signature still occupies the window.
findings.suggested_fix: Since ARQ/Redis is already a hard dependency of this feature, back this one key with Redis rather than the in-process dict (the module docstring already names this migration). Minimal interim steps if that is deferred: (1) validate `_check_sig` *before* the rate-limit check so unsigned scans never consume a window, and (2) bound `_WINDOW_STATE` by evicting keys not seen within a few windows on each call (or cap total keys and reset wholesale when exceeded) so unauthenticated key churn cannot grow memory without limit.

findings.title: IntegrityError recovery rolls back the whole transaction
findings.why_it_matters: Both dedup-race handlers in `report_service` treat `IntegrityError` as if it only undid their own INSERT, but `Session.rollback()` rolls back the entire transaction, not a statement. In `execute_definition_task` the enclosing transaction also carries the `task_row.status='RUNNING'` update, the whole `builder_service.execute_definition` result set, and the `condition_snapshot`/`row_count` updates it flushed. If two projects render byte-identical custom reports concurrently (same rows, same style — the content hash is deterministic by design), the loser's `db.rollback()` at line 444 silently discards the execution-log snapshot it just computed; the caller then commits a half-done unit of work that looks successful. The same pattern in `ensure_pending_row:325` has the same shape. The correct primitive for 'my insert lost a race, retry as read' is `db.begin_nested()` (SAVEPOINT), which confines the damage to the failing INSERT.
evidence: pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:442-447 — `    except IntegrityError:` / `        # 并发下另一个请求刚插了同一 content_hash —— 回滚自己的插入，复用它的` / `        await db.rollback()` / `        return (await db.execute(` — the comment claims a statement-scoped undo; `Session.rollback()` is transaction-scoped.
pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:443 — `        # 并发下另一个请求刚插了同一 content_hash —— 回滚自己的插入，复用它的` — the intent is explicitly narrower than what the code does.

pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:277 — `    await db.flush()` (end of `builder_service.execute_definition`, which wrote the reproducible `condition_snapshot` into the same transaction) — collateral damage from the rollback at line 444.
Same shape at pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:325 — `        await db.rollback()` inside `ensure_pending_row`'s IntegrityError handler.
pcs-backend/app/workers/report_builder_tasks.py:96 — `            await db.commit()` — the task commits whatever survived, with no check that the log-row updates it expected are still present.

findings.title: Deterministic .part temp path collides on concurrent identical renders
findings.why_it_matters: Files are content-addressed (`{hash[:16]}.{ext}`) and the temp file is derived deterministically from the destination, so every concurrent render of the same content targets the *same* `.part` path. `_write_file` runs in a thread via `asyncio.to_thread`, so two ARQ jobs can genuinely interleave: A writes `.part`, B opens `.part` with 'wb' (truncating), A calls `tmp.replace(abs_path)` removing the temp name, and B's `replace` then raises `FileNotFoundError`. That surfaces as an `OSError` → converted to `PcsError(code='REPORT_STORAGE_FAILED', status=500)`, the task is marked FAILED and audited as a report failure, even though the byte-identical file is already correctly published by A. The trigger is narrow (identical content across two projects/users rendering simultaneously) but the hashing-by-design makes it plausible, and a spurious FAILED is worse than a shared temp file. A unique temp name (uuid per call) removes it entirely.
evidence: pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:271-273 — `    tmp = abs_path.with_suffix(abs_path.suffix + ".part")` / `    tmp.write_bytes(payload)` / `    tmp.replace(abs_path)` — the temp name is a pure function of the destination, so two writers of the same digest collide on it.

pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:390 — `    relpath = paths.new_file_path(digest, _EXT[output_format])` — and paths.py:58 `    return f"{content_hash[:16]}.{ext}"`, i.e. the destination is content-addressed, which is precisely the condition for two jobs to pick the same path.
pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:371 — `        payload = await asyncio.to_thread(` — the write runs in a worker thread, so the interleaving is real rather than hypothetical.

pcs-backend/app/services/report/report_service.py:393-404 — `    except OSError as e:` … `            code="REPORT_STORAGE_FAILED", status=500,` — a lost rename race is reported as a storage failure and drives the task to FAILED.
findings.suggested_fix:
Make the temp name unique per call so concurrent writers never share it:

```python
import uuid
...
    abs_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    tmp = abs_path.with_name(f"{abs_path.name}.{uuid.uuid4().hex}.part")
    try:
        tmp.write_bytes(payload)
        tmp.replace(abs_path)
    except OSError:
        tmp.unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise
```
The `unlink` in the handler additionally fixes the leftover `.part` files that a failed rename currently leaves behind forever (nothing in the module cleans them up, and `resolve_path` does not filter `.part` — they sit inside the storage root).

residual_risks: Renderers are CPU-bound and run via `asyncio.to_thread` with `WorkerSettings.max_jobs = 4`. ReportLab/python-docx/openpyxl hold the GIL for much of their work, so four concurrent 10k-row renders can stall the worker's event loop, delaying `job_timeout = 300` expiry handling, the reclaim cron, and job pickup simultaneously. No measurement or concurrency cap exists in this diff to bound it.

File-then-DB ordering in `store_rendered` (report_service.py:392 writes the file, :406 upserts the row) leaves an orphan file on disk whenever the subsequent commit fails. The code acknowledges this for the audit-write case (:419-421) but not for a commit failure in the enclosing task; nothing sweeps orphaned files whose content_hash has no report_files row.

`_write_file` leaves `.part` temporaries on disk whenever `write_bytes` succeeds but `replace` fails. Nothing enumerates or cleans them, so repeated render failures accumulate unattributable bytes in the storage root.

The reclaimer relies solely on a heartbeat threshold (`STALE_MINUTES = 15`) rather than an owner token. There is no way for a genuinely long-running render (large custom definition, slow DB) to signal liveness, so a legitimately slow job past 15 minutes is indistinguishable from a killed one. `execute_definition_task` sets RUNNING once and never refreshes `updated_at` during rendering.

`reclaim_stale_tasks` selects PENDING rows without `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and its transaction stays open across the audit writes in the loop. Two worker processes running the cron simultaneously (CronJob `unique=False`) can both select and both write the same rows; the audit table will show duplicate RECLAIMED entries for one task.

grep-only coverage note: `paths.py`, `renderer_pdf.py`, `renderer_docx.py`, `renderer_xlsx.py` and `collector.py` were reviewed by reading their changed surface, but the review did not exhaustively enumerate every exception handler in the three renderer modules (≈31 KB combined); error handling in the XLSX/DOCX cell-formatting branches is unverified.
testing_gaps: No test drives the reclaim path through `reclaim_stale_report_tasks(ctx)` and then reads `ReportFile.status` / `ReportExecutionLog.status` from a separate session — the exact `_is_committed` pattern already used for the task bodies. Every reclaim test passes the fixture session directly, which is why the missing commit is invisible.

No test asserts that a successful `execute_definition_task` leaves the execution log in a state the reclaimer's `status IN ('QUEUED','RUNNING')` filter will not match, i.e. there is no test that a completed run survives a subsequent `reclaim_stale_execution_logs` call with `condition_snapshot` intact.

No end-to-end test goes from a rendered PDF's QR payload to the verify endpoint. tests/api/v1/test_report.py hand-builds the HMAC signature itself, so no test would fail if the QR stopped carrying one or if `qr_payload` stayed `None` in `report_service._render_sync`.

No test covers the builder execute endpoint's ordering under a fast worker: there is no scenario where the ARQ job is made to start (or a session hook to delay the commit) before the ReportExecutionLog insert commits, so the enqueue-before-commit race is unexercised.

No failure-injection test for `enqueue_job` raising on the builder path — the 503 path from `_enqueue` that would leave a committed orphan QUEUED log row is untested (the report.py path has `_fail_pending`, the builder path has no equivalent).
